Case Study · Internal Tool · Production Pipeline Design

MOCAPFLOW

MocapFlow is an internal production tool for teams creating large volumes of 3D character animations. In our case, 4 people had to coordinate 1,800+ motion-captured assets that needed to be cleaned, reviewed, versioned, and integrated into game engines. The technical production worked, but the operating layer around it did not: status, feedback, and validation lived across disconnected tools and depended on manual coordination.

RoleProduct Designer
TypeInternal Tool
Team4 people
Context3D Animation Pipeline

TL;DR

This project started as a workflow pain point, but the diagnosis revealed a product problem: no source of truth, no reliable state model, and too much coordination overhead for a 4-person team managing 1,800+ animation assets. I designed a dedicated internal tool that turned review, feedback, versioning, and status into one connected system. The outcome was not just faster validation, but a more trustworthy operating model.

Core Insight

The production pipeline worked technically. The failure point was the operating model around it. Status lived in one place, files in another, feedback in another, and validation in external tools. The result was not mere disorganization but a system with high coordination cost and no trustworthy operational state.

01 — Problem

A real production.
A fragile system.

In an independent studio of 4 people, we produced over 1,800 motion-captured animation assets for integration into game engines via the Unreal Engine and Unity marketplaces.

The technical pipeline worked: motion capture recording, animation cleanup, engine integration. What failed was the layer that turned production into a reliable workflow: planning, review, feedback traceability, and status coherence.

The coordination challenge was amplified by the fact that two user groups depended on the same system for very different purposes: Animators needed fast execution and clear next actions, while Lead Animators needed trustworthy validation and oversight.

The stack

Google Drive stored files. Google Sheets tracked progress. Discord carried review feedback. Each tool was usable in isolation, but none owned the full lifecycle of an animation. There was no single source of truth, only partial truths spread across tools.

The real question

How do you design a system in which the operational state is generated by user actions, instead of relying on people to manually keep multiple tools synchronized?

⚠ Problem 01

Tracking was wrong by design

Status updates were manual. Any delay created drift between the spreadsheet and reality. The issue was not discipline, but a non-self-healing system that depended on human synchronization.

⚠ Problem 02

Feedback was disconnected from work

Reviews happened on Discord, detached from the exact file version they referred to, then buried in chat history. Feedback existed, but not as actionable production data.

⚠ Problem 03

Validation happened out of context

Validation required downloading the file, opening an external tool, then returning elsewhere to comment and update status. The decision layer was decoupled from the artifact, which made review slower and less reliable.

⚠ Problem 04

Constant dependency on the lead

Because no status was trustworthy and no feedback trail was stable, the lead had to continuously reconstruct reality by hand. The bottleneck was structural, not managerial.

02 — Diagnosis

Optimize the existing
or rebuild from scratch?

Before choosing a solution, I mapped the real production flow: where work moved, where it stalled, and where information changed state without being captured anywhere. That diagnosis made the decision binary: optimize fragmented tools, or redesign the system model itself.

Option A

Optimize the existing stack

  • Better-organized Drive structure
  • Stricter Sheet conventions
  • Formalized Discord rules

✕ Faster and cheaper. But it preserves fragmentation, manual state reconciliation, and lead dependency.

Option B — Chosen

Build a dedicated product

  • Connect information across the pipeline
  • Structure actions around the animation as the central unit
  • Reduce human coordination dependency

✓ Higher upfront cost, but structurally sound. The animation becomes the system object; status, review, and history become consequences of actions around it.

Strategic decision

I chose not to optimize a fragmented workflow but to redesign the system around the animation itself. That meant accepting more build complexity in exchange for lower coordination cost, stronger traceability, and a state model the team could trust without manual reconciliation.

What we could have done

  • Stricter spreadsheet governance
  • Folder naming conventions
  • Discord review rituals and manual checklists

Why that was rejected

  • Improves behavior, not system logic
  • Still requires people to keep tools aligned manually
  • Becomes more fragile as asset volume grows
03 — Key Design Decisions

Not features.
Positions.

Every major design decision was a trade-off between flexibility and reliability. I optimized for system coherence first, then for interface convenience. That meant deliberately removing some manual freedom when that freedom was the source of operational drift.

01Integrate a 3D viewer

Problem

Validation required downloading files and opening MotionBuilder or Unreal Engine. Context-switching destroyed review efficiency.

Decision

Build a 3D FBX viewer directly into the review workspace. Visualization, decision, feedback, and status update all in one place.

Trade-off accepted

Higher technical complexity. More development cost. Narrower browser compatibility.

Without this, the product would have remained an administrative layer on top of the old workflow. The viewer turns review into a first-class product action instead of an external ritual.
02Actionable inbox only

Problem

Feedback was scattered across Discord threads. Animators couldn't reliably find what needed fixing.

Decision

Inbox shows only animations that require action: rejected items with attached feedback. No general notifications. No noise.

Trade-off accepted

Loss of exhaustiveness. Users see less in the inbox.

The gain is not completeness but decisiveness. Users no longer browse for context; the system surfaces only work that can be acted on immediately.
▶ Design iteration The inbox was not always like this.

V1 — Notification model

Full visibility. Everything visible.

Uploads, comments, approvals, rejections — all surfaced as notifications, similar to Slack or a task manager.

✕ Animators still had to scan multiple signals, identify what required action, and manually prioritize. We had recreated the same problem inside a new interface.

V2 — Action model

Visibility of what requires action only.

Only rejected items appear in the inbox. Full activity history moved to a separate dashboard feed. Two surfaces, two distinct jobs.

✓ The inbox became execution-focused. The dashboard preserved traceability. No signal was lost — it just moved to the right surface.

Trade-off accepted: reduced exhaustiveness in the inbox in exchange for a significant gain in clarity and speed. An animator should never have to decide what to act on — the system should make that obvious.

Why this screen matters

The inbox operationalizes one of the core product decisions: feedback is not treated as generic notification noise, but as structured work to resolve. Grouping by pack preserves scanability, while expansion reveals the exact animation and comment that requires attention.

03Automated status system

Problem

Statuses were manually updated. Delays and omissions created constant desynchronization between the Sheet and reality.

Decision

Status is a consequence of an action. Upload sets 'Pending'. Approval sets 'Approved'. Rejection triggers feedback and sets 'To Modify'.

Trade-off accepted

Less manual control over status.

This converts status from editable metadata into system output. The recorded state now reflects what actually happened, not what someone remembered to update.

Why these screens matter

These two states make the automation legible inside the roadmap itself. The interface does not ask users to maintain status as separate admin work; it reflects operational changes triggered by assignment and workflow events, which turns the roadmap into a more trustworthy source of truth.

Lifecycle logic

The roadmap screens show where status is visible in the interface. This diagram explains the underlying model: every animation follows a controlled lifecycle, and rejected assets re-enter the loop at the right production stage instead of becoming disconnected feedback items.

04Separate pipeline moments

Problem

Mixing planning, production, and validation in one interface would have created cognitive overload similar to the original spreadsheet.

Decision

Three distinct zones inside each project: Roadmap (plan), Upload (execute), Review (decide). Each moment has its own context.

Trade-off accepted

Reduced compactness. More navigation steps.

This preserves contextual integrity. Planning, producing, and validating involve different decisions, so collapsing them into one surface would have reintroduced the ambiguity the product was meant to remove.
05Versioning tied to animation ID

Problem

File naming was manual and inconsistent. Multiple versions of the same animation coexisted without clear history.

Decision

Each uploaded file is linked to the animation ID defined in the roadmap. Versions are created automatically with full history.

Trade-off accepted

More system complexity. Requires discipline in roadmap setup.

This eliminates ambiguity at the object level. Instead of naming discipline, the system enforces continuity between animation ID, current file, and version history.
04 — Product Architecture

Structure without
overwhelming.

The main challenge was not adding features. It was deciding which information belonged together and which did not. With projects, animations, statuses, feedback, versions, and deadlines all in play, a single unified view would have recreated the exact cognitive overload of the spreadsheet we were replacing.

Surface 01

Dashboard

Operational overview

  • Active projects at a glance
  • Team workload distribution
  • Deadline countdowns per project
  • Priority alerts surfaced automatically
Surface 02

Project (3 tabs)

State by workflow moment

  • Roadmap: assign animations, set priorities
  • Upload: submit files, link to animation ID
  • Review: 3D viewer, approve or reject, write feedback
Surface 03

Inbox

Action queue, not feed

  • Only rejected animations with feedback
  • No general notifications
  • No inbox zero pressure
  • Every item is an action, not information
05 — Impact

What changed.
What stayed the same.

Methodology note

Impact is based on internal observation, not instrumented analytics. The estimates come from recurring coordination tasks that existed before the redesign: locating the right file, retrieving review comments, confirming current status, and rechecking version history. Where precision is not available, the numbers are framed as operational estimates rather than hard performance claims.

AreaBefore / AfterResultSource
3D Viewer Lead had to open MotionBuilder or Unreal for each review. Integrated viewer eliminates that context switch entirely. ~15–20 min/day Internal estimate
Inbox Feedback was scattered across Discord threads. Actionable inbox surfaces only what requires action, immediately. ~10–15 min/day Internal estimate
Status tracking Manual status updates in Sheets created frequent drift. Automated transitions remove the reconciliation loop entirely. ~5–10 min/day Internal estimate
Total saved Across viewer, inbox, and status tasks — 5 to 7 coordination actions per person per day eliminated. ~30–45 min/day Internal estimate
Versioning Manual file naming caused frequent ambiguity. Now each file links to an animation ID with automatic history. Structured Observed
Lead dependency Lead no longer reconstructs pipeline reality manually. System state surfaces automatically from workflow events. Reduced Observed

Principal gain

The most important outcome is not the estimated time saved. It is that the team no longer needs to constantly reconstruct reality across tools. The product reduces coordination overhead by making state, feedback, and validation legible in one operating model.

06 — Limits & Trade-offs

What this does not solve.

This system was designed for a small team with clearly defined roles. Some constraints are worth naming honestly.

Scaling to larger teams requires rethinking permissions.

The current model assumes a small team with low organizational distance. At larger scale, multi-step approvals, supervisor layers, and granular permissions would be required. The challenge would be to add governance without reintroducing coordination drag.

The 3D viewer has real technical constraints.

Browser-based FBX rendering is computationally expensive. At higher volumes, file size, load performance, and infrastructure cost would become product constraints, not just technical ones. The strongest feature is also the most likely scaling risk.

Impact measurement remains qualitative.

The 30–45 minute estimate is derived from repeated coordination tasks, not product analytics. A production-grade rollout should instrument review duration, rework frequency, approval latency, and version churn per asset to convert operational intuition into hard product evidence.

07 — Learnings

What this project
taught me.

The central object defines the architecture — not the other way around.

When we started mapping the pipeline, we tried to fit animations into a generic task model. It immediately broke down: an animation is not a task, it must be seen and interpreted before a decision can be made. Once we accepted that, the entire architecture realigned — the viewer became non-negotiable, the inbox became action-based, and review became a product-first action rather than an external ritual.

A notification model is not always a visibility model.

Our first inbox design showed everything. It felt comprehensive. In real usage, animators still had to scan, filter, and prioritize manually — the same problem we were trying to solve, reproduced inside a new interface. The shift to an action-only inbox was the single design decision that most directly reduced daily friction. Completeness and actionability are not the same thing. We had to choose one.

Reliability is a product feature, not a side effect.

Automated status transitions felt like a constraint when we designed them. In practice, they were the most impactful part of the system. When the lead can trust the pipeline state without verifying it manually, the entire operating model changes. Removing degrees of freedom that mainly generate mistakes is a product decision, not a compromise.

When fragmentation is the root cause, optimization is a band-aid.

We had enough data to make the spreadsheet work better. Tighter naming conventions, clearer Discord threads, more disciplined Drive structure. We modeled what that would look like. It would have required 3 manual synchronizations per animation cycle just to keep status consistent across tools. That analysis made rebuilding the only architecturally honest option — not a preference, a structural conclusion.
